opus-5.5.text:
I'm incredibly proud of the team. Interpretability is still a young field, so there aren't many people in the world who've done serious, frontier-level work on it, and we've been fortunate to bring a number of them together under one roof. We have researchers who helped pioneer some of the core techniques, like sparse autoencoders and mechanistic circuit analysis, people who came out of places like DeepMind and OpenAI and from strong academic labs, and who've really shaped how the field thinks about decomposing what's happening inside neural networks.

What I think makes the team special, though, isn't just the research pedigree. It's the combination. You need people who can do rigorous, curiosity-driven science, because we're genuinely trying to understand something nobody fully understands yet. But you also need excellent engineers, because doing interpretability at scale on frontier-sized models is a massive infrastructure problem. You're training dictionaries with millions of features, storing and serving huge volumes of activations, building tools so people can actually explore and intervene on models. And then you need people with product sense who can take those research breakthroughs and turn them into something useful for developers and enterprises.

Getting those three groups to work closely together, rather than research throwing papers over the wall, has been a big focus for us. The tight loop between understanding a model, building tools around that understanding, and seeing how people use it in practice is, I think, where a lot of the progress is going to come from.

And honestly, there's a shared sense of mission. Everyone here believes that as these models get more powerful, being able to look inside them, understand them, and steer them precisely is one of the most important problems we could be working on. That conviction makes it a really special group to be part of.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the team is the thing I'm proudest of, and it's also the thing I'd point to as our real edge.

When we started Goodfire, the bet was that interpretability was about to go from a research curiosity to something you could actually build a company around. But to do that, you can't just hire great ML researchers, and you can't just hire great engineers. You need both, and you need people who can live in the gap between them. So the team is a mix: people who came out of places like Anthropic, DeepMind, OpenAI, and academic labs where they'd been doing mechanistic interpretability work for years, alongside folks who've shipped real products and infrastructure at scale.

What I look for is a particular kind of person. They're deeply technical, they have genuine scientific taste, meaning they know which problems are worth working on and which are dead ends, and they also care about this stuff actually getting used. A lot of interpretability work historically has been beautiful and has not touched a single production model. We want to change that, and that requires people who get a little impatient with research that doesn't ship.

The other thing I'd say is that it's a small team by design. Interpretability is still early enough that the leverage is in ideas, not headcount. A handful of people who really understand how to find features in a model, steer them, and turn that into something a developer can use will outperform a much larger team that's just throwing compute at it. So we've been very deliberate about staying lean and keeping the bar extremely high.

If I'm being self-critical, the risk with a team like this is that you can get too enamored with the science and lose sight of the customer. So part of my job is keeping us honest about that, making sure every research direction has a line of sight to someone who actually needs it.
